title: Keep Running Through the Hard Parts
overview: The writer urges weary believers to keep going by looking to Jesus, to see their hardships as a father's training, and to remember the awe and hope of what they have been brought into.

parts.label: The race and its leader (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The "cloud of witnesses" are the people of faith from chapter 11, pictured like a crowd around runners in a race, and readers are urged to drop whatever slows them and fix their eyes on Jesus, who went first and finished. He endured the shame of the cross because he looked ahead to the joy beyond it.

parts.label: Hardship as training (vv. 4-11)
parts.note: The readers had suffered loss and insult but had not yet been killed for their faith, and the writer quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 to say God trains those he treats as his own children. Like a good parent's correction, it hurts at the time but is meant to grow goodness and peace later.

parts.label: Steady yourselves and each other (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Weary people are told to strengthen themselves so the weakest among them are helped rather than hurt, and to keep bitterness from spreading through the group. Esau traded his rights as the oldest son for one meal (Genesis 25) and was later turned away despite tears, though translations differ on whether he was seeking the blessing itself or a change of mind, possibly his father's.

parts.label: Two mountains compared (vv. 18-24)
parts.note: Mount Sinai, where God gave Israel the law amid fire, darkness and a terrifying voice (Exodus 19), is set against Mount Zion, a picture of heaven where God, angels and the faithful gather in celebration. Abel's blood cried out from the ground after his brother killed him (Genesis 4), and the writer says the blood of Jesus, the go-between of a new covenant (a new agreement between God and people), speaks something better.

parts.label: What cannot be shaken (vv. 25-29)
parts.note: Quoting Haggai 2:6, the writer says God will one day shake the whole created world so that only what is lasting remains, and his people are receiving a kingdom that will survive it. The fitting response is gratitude and worship with awe, because "God is a consuming fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24), a way of saying God is holy and not to be taken lightly.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether warnings like Esau's and the call not to refuse God mean a true believer can fall away for good, or describe people who never truly belonged in the first place.
think: Looking back on something painful in your life, did it end up shaping you in ways you value, or was it simply loss?
